summary: Gives basic recommendations for running a country-level X.500 Directory Service Agent as part of a production directory service. It is informational guidance rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Advice for a country on how to run its part of a giant phone book so it works well with everyone else's.

questions: how to run an x.500 production directory
recommendations for country level x.500 dsa
what is a dsa in x.500
subtitle: Basic service targets for running a country-level X.500 directory server as a production service rather than a pilot.

tldr.problem: Parts of the global X.500 directory were still run as pilot projects, with poor availability and inconsistent information quality, partly because there were no formal service objectives.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out recommendations for the country-level master DSA, for service providers and staff, for DSAs in the national directory, and for DSA software.
tldr.outcome: It calls these recommendations only a starting point toward a production-quality X.500 infrastructure. It is an Informational memo, not a standard.

today: RFC 1803 is an Informational memo, not a standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself calls its advice a starting point.

sections.title: Why a Production Directory Is Needed
sections.content:
The ISO/CCITT X.500 Directory standard allows a single world-wide Directory holding information about many things, including people. In mid 1989 NYSERNet, later taken over by Performance Systems International (PSI), started a White-pages Pilot Project in the United States. In November 1990 the PARADISE project began in Europe and ran the "root of the world" DSA that joined the national pilots into one world-wide Directory Information Tree (DIT).

The memo says much of the criticism of X.500 comes from the lack of a production-quality infrastructure. There were already well over 500 organizations and 1,000,000 entries, yet some portions were still considered pilots, with poor availability and inconsistent information quality. Because country-level DSAs are the access path for the rest of the world, their availability and performance set an upper bound on the quality of the whole country's part of the Directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The big phone book worked, but some parts were slow, sometimes offline or out of date. Since everyone reaches a country's listings through one main doorway, that doorway has to be dependable.

sections.title: Running the Country-Level Master and Shadow DSAs
sections.content:
Country-level data should be available for querying 100% of the time. Updating may be slightly less available because X.500 uses a single master scheme. The master DSA should be available at least 95% of the time, which means monitoring and support over the weekend.

The master and its shadow DSAs should be placed to avoid single points of failure and dispersed across the national network to spread load and bring information closer to requesters. Country DIT information, including naming infrastructure such as localities and states, should be replicated across the oceans. For instance, there should be a complete copy of the US root in Europe and a copy of the Japanese root in Africa and North America. The master and shadows must run software that meets the recommendations in section 4 of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The main copy of the phone book should almost always be open, and copies should be kept in different places so one broken link does not shut everyone out.

sections.title: Service Provider and Staff Recommendations
sections.content:
The service provider should publish a generic e-mail address for the DSA manager, with more than one manager available. Response times are specific: mail to the manager acknowledged within one working day; trouble reports on the master and shadow DSAs answered within 24 hours, with a resolution where possible; general informational requests acknowledged within 2 working days. Changes to the national master DSA should be turned around in 2 working days, with acknowledgment within 1 working day.

The provider should keep a current mailing list of all DSA managers in the country, document how to join and which software to run, and drop references to "pilot" with a transition plan. Organizations that do not meet the published guidelines should be removed after at least 4 weeks' notice, with the procedure run at least once every 3 months and a 3-month grace period for new organizations. In North America the service should act as an ADDMD in the North American Directory Forum, so Internet X.500 and NADF X.500 share one consistent DIT.

For personnel, the memo asks for a help desk, quarterly status reports on the state of the service, and electronic access to service information such as a World Wide Web page and FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The keepers must answer emails quickly, tell people how to join, publish reports, and politely remove members who do not follow the rules after giving them time to fix things.

sections.title: Rules for DSAs and Their Software
sections.content:
Every DSA in the country-level Directory Management Domain should keep its organization's subtree available as close to 100% as possible, using a master DSA and zero or more shadows. Information should be complete, accurate and up to date, and reachable through Directory protocols as far as the organization's security and privacy policies allow. Two contact persons must be named as managers for each DSA.

Organizations still experimenting should be marked clearly as "experimental", for example through a Quality of Service attribute or the word in the organization's RDN, or listed in a separate, clearly marked part of the namespace until they move to the production DIT.

DSA software should support the attributes and object classes of the Internet schema in RFC 1274, and be reliable, supportable and fast enough for the DSA traffic. The service provider may add requirements, such as '93 replication.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who runs a piece of the phone book must keep it correct and online, name two people to call, and label test entries so nobody mistakes them for real ones.

sections.title: Security and Open Work
sections.content: The memo states that security issues are not discussed. It calls its recommendations only a starting point. A truly production-quality X.500 infrastructure needs more work, including a transition from the 1988 X.500 plus Internet extensions to the 1993 X.500 standard with its replication and knowledge model. The memo does not discuss that transition.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not cover safety, and it says this is just a first set of rules with more work to do.
